questions.q: Define consumer responsibility and give one example that is NOT simply “complaining when cheated.”
questions.a: Consumer responsibility is a proactive duty a buyer must fulfil to protect themselves and the market, e.g., checking the ISI mark on an electrical appliance before purchase. A wrong answer that only mentions “filing a complaint after being cheated” reveals the misconception that responsibilities are reactive rather than preventive.

questions.q: Explain in your own words why consumer education is needed even when the Consumer Protection Act grants six legal rights.
questions.a: Legal rights exist on paper, but consumers need education to know those rights, understand complex product information, navigate digital markets, and act before harm occurs. An answer that says “rights are enough” shows the student misses the gap between legal entitlement and practical ability to exercise it.

questions.q: A consumer buys a “100% natural” face cream online without checking for a licence number or reading reviews. She develops a rash. Identify TWO specific responsibilities she neglected and state what she should have done instead.
questions.a: Neglected responsibilities: (1) Being informed — she should have verified the product’s licence/certification and ingredient list; (2) Being cautious — she should have read independent reviews and done a patch test. A response blaming only the seller misses the shared accountability central to consumer responsibility.

questions.q: Compare the scope of consumer education in a rural village versus an urban metro. Identify two overlaps and two differences.
questions.a: Overlaps: basic rights awareness, redressal mechanisms. Differences: rural scope emphasises adulteration detection, weights/measures, and government scheme literacy; urban scope adds digital payments security, e‑commerce return policies, and sustainable packaging choices. An answer listing only topics without contextualising them shows inability to analyse scope dynamically.

questions.q: Evaluate this statement: “Consumer education is only for people who have been cheated.” Provide a reasoned judgement.
questions.a: The statement is false. Consumer education is preventive — it builds skills to avoid exploitation, promotes sustainable habits, and empowers collective action. A student who agrees reveals a reactive mindset and confuses education with redressal.

questions.q: Design a one‑page poster for a school campaign that teaches students three consumer responsibilities relevant to buying packaged snacks. Include a catchy slogan, one visual metaphor, and a QR‑code placeholder for a video.
questions.a: A strong answer includes: slogan like “Check, Choose, Change”, visual of a magnifying glass over a label, three responsibilities (read label, demand bill, dispose wrapper responsibly), and a QR box labelled “Scan for 60‑sec label‑reading demo.” A weak answer lists rights instead of responsibilities or omits actionable steps.
